messages.content: Write a conference talk abstract for a talk about moving a monolith to microservices. Around 200 words.

**Title:** We Split the Monolith Into 40 Services. Six Would Have Been Enough.

Three years ago our billing system was 900,000 lines of Java, one deploy a week, and a test suite that took 51 minutes to tell us nothing. Today it's 40 services. I think we overshot by about 34.

This is the unglamorous version of that migration. I'll walk through the three extractions that paid for themselves — payments, notifications, and the fraud scorer — and show the metrics that justified them: p99 latency, deploy frequency, and how many people had to be in a room to ship a change. Then I'll walk through the ones that didn't. Splitting the customer record across four services cost us eight months and bought a distributed transaction we still work around with a nightly reconciliation job.

You'll leave with a test you can apply on Monday: for each candidate service, name the team that owns it and the deploy it unblocks. If you can't do both, don't cut there. Service boundaries are org boundaries wearing a network hop, and a network hop you didn't need is just latency with extra alerting.

Come argue with me afterward. I've changed my mind on this twice.

Swap the numbers for your own — the shape holds, but the specifics are what make an abstract land with a program committee.

**Title:** Forty Services Later: We Only Needed Six

Three years ago, billing was 900,000 lines of Java, one release a week, and a 51-minute test suite that caught nothing. It's 40 services now. My guess is that 34 of them were a mistake.

This is the boring account of how that happened. I'll cover the three extractions that earned their keep (payments, notifications, the fraud scorer) and the numbers that backed them: p99 latency, release cadence, and how many people had to be in the room to ship one change. Then the failures. Spreading the customer record across four services burned eight months and left us with a distributed transaction we still paper over using a nightly reconciliation job.

You'll go home with one question to ask about every proposed service: which team owns it, and which deploy does it unblock? If you can't answer both, don't cut there. Service boundaries are org boundaries with a network hop stapled on, and a hop you didn't need is just latency plus more pages at 3am.

Find me in the hallway and tell me I'm wrong. I've flipped positions on this twice already.
